back: The atom/group that gives a compound its characteristic chemical properties.

front: Suffixes: alcohol, aldehyde, ketone, carboxylic acid, ester?
back: -ol, -al, -one, -oic acid, -oate.
Same functional group and general formula, differ by CH₂, similar chemistry, trend in physical properties.

front: Effect of chain length and branching on boiling point?
back: Longer chain → higher bp; more branching → lower bp (London forces).
Longest chain with group → suffix → lowest locant for group → alphabetical substituent prefixes.
C bearing OH bonded to 1, 2 or 3 other carbons.
Chain, position, functional group.
Restricted rotation (C=C or ring) and two different groups on each relevant carbon.
C with four different groups; enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images rotating plane-polarised light oppositely.
((2C + 2 + N) − (H + X))/2 = rings + π bonds.
O–H alcohol 3200–3600 broad; O–H acid 2500–3000 very broad; C=O 1700–1750.

front: (HL) What does ¹H NMR tell you?
back: Signals = environments; shift = type; integration = number of H; n + 1 splitting = neighbouring H.

front: Molecular vs structural vs skeletal formula?
back: Molecular: atoms present (C₂H₆O). Condensed structural: CH₃CH₂OH. Full structural: every bond shown. Skeletal: lines for C chain, H on C omitted.

front: General formulas of alkanes, alkenes, alcohols, carboxylic acids?
back: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; CₙH₂ₙ; CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH; CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH.
Aldehyde (carbonyl), ketone (carbonyl), carboxylic acid (carboxyl), ester, amine (amino), amide (amido).

front: Halogenoalkane and ether: functional group and naming?
back: Halogenoalkane: C–X, prefix fluoro/chloro/bromo/iodo (2-bromopropane). Ether: C–O–C, named as alkoxy-alkane (methoxyethane).
Alkyl group from the alcohol first, then acid part with -oate: ethyl ethanoate.
N bonded to 1, 2 or 3 carbon (alkyl) groups: CH₃NH₂ (1°), (CH₃)₂NH (2°), (CH₃)₃N (3°).

front: Boiling point order for similar Mr: alkane, aldehyde, alcohol, carboxylic acid?
back: Alkane < aldehyde < alcohol < carboxylic acid — London only; dipole–dipole; H-bonding; stronger H-bonding (dimers).

front: Why does water solubility of alcohols decrease as chain length increases?
back: The non-polar hydrocarbon chain grows while the single –OH H-bonding group stays the same.
Propanal CH₃CH₂CHO (aldehyde) and propanone CH₃COCH₃ (ketone).
Butane and 2-methylpropane (chain isomers).
cis: both CH₃ groups on the same side of C=C. trans: on opposite sides. They differ in physical properties (e.g. bp, mp).
Identical physical and chemical properties except: rotate plane-polarised light equally in opposite directions, and react differently with other chiral molecules (e.g. enzymes).
Equimolar mixture of two enantiomers; optically inactive because the rotations cancel.
Polarimeter: each enantiomer rotates the plane of plane-polarised light by the same angle in opposite directions.
m/z 15 CH₃⁺, 29 C₂H₅⁺/CHO⁺, 31 CH₂OH⁺, 43 C₃H₇⁺/CH₃CO⁺, 45 COOH⁺; the M⁺ peak (highest m/z) gives the molar mass.

front: (HL) Why do bonds absorb IR radiation?
back: Bonds vibrate (stretch/bend) at specific frequencies; absorption occurs when the vibration changes the molecular dipole moment. Wavenumbers in cm⁻¹.

front: (HL) Why is CO₂ a greenhouse gas though it is non-polar?
back: Its asymmetric stretch and bending vibrations change the dipole moment, so it absorbs IR; symmetric stretch is IR inactive.

front: (HL) Role of TMS in ¹H NMR?
back: Tetramethylsilane Si(CH₃)₄ is the reference (δ = 0 ppm): 12 equivalent H give one strong signal upfield; inert and volatile.
R–CH₃ 0.9–1.0; CH₃–C=O 2.0–2.5; –CH₂–O 3.3–3.7; R–CHO 9.4–10; –COOH 9.0–13.0 ppm (see data booklet).

front: (HL) Splitting pattern of ethyl group CH₃CH₂–?
back: CH₃: triplet (2 neighbouring H, n + 1 = 3). CH₂: quartet (3 neighbouring H). OH protons usually don’t split.
Three signals, integration 3 : 2 : 1 (CH₃ triplet, CH₂ quartet, OH singlet).

front: (HL) IHD of C₆H₆ and what it means?
back: (2×6 + 2 − 6)/2 = 4: one ring + three π bonds (benzene).
